newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Half of Austrians want political change - survey.
newsitem.headline: Half of Austrians want political change - survey.

text.p: More than 50 percent of Austrians are unhappy with their government, a survey showed on Monday -- just two months after the ruling Social Democrats slumped to an all-time low in European Parliament elections.
Joerg Haider's far-right Freedom Party scored their record high in the election, with nearly 28 percent of the vote, finishing just 60,000 votes behind the Social Democrats.

The Linz-based research institute Market, which carried out the survey for the daily Standard, said 52 percent of men and 60 percent of women agreed that there was a need for new policy ideas from the government.
A total of 52 percent said they were dissatisfied with the direction in which Austria was moving.
Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats rule in a sometimes uneasy coalition with their junior partner, the conservative People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel.

Market interviewed 1,000 people to compile the opinion poll, which backed up findings in a separate survey conducted by Market last month. It which showed only eight percent of Austrians believed the government was doing a good job.
In the aftermath of the European elections, political analysts said many Austrians were disenchanted with the European Union, which the Alpine republic joined two years ago.
Membership has coincided with an economic slowdown, rising unemployment, factory closures and record company insolvencies and takeovers.

Some 50 percent of blue-collar voters backed Haider's far right in the European elections, switching allegiance from the Social Democrats. The government parties are united in support of the EU and further integration.
Haider campaigned against the Maastricht Treaty on European economic and monetary union and a single currency, blaming most of Austria's economic woes on EU membership.
